title: Future Guelph annual progress report
subtitle: Local boards report on 2025: downtown events, Elliott Community, conservation lands, library, police and public health.
overview: Council held a special meeting to review the city's annual Future Guelph Strategic Plan progress report for 2025, the second full year of the plan. Council received the report {{vote:m1}}. Staff said about two-thirds of foundations initiatives and half of city building and environment initiatives were on track. Housing construction slowed, and greenhouse gas reductions have not reached targets.

Staff highlighted the credit rating, the community planning permit system, the South End Community Centre and Baker Library projects, and downtown renewal work. They also described plans to move to more real-time progress reporting and to refresh the strategic plan for the next term of council.

Representatives of the Downtown Guelph Business Association, The Elliott Community, the Grand River Conservation Authority, Guelph Public Library, Guelph Police Services and Wellington Dufferin Guelph Public Health each presented. Council also approved a by-law {{vote:m2}} and adjourned. The mayor said this is the last council meeting for a while, apart from a possible short one in August.

decisions.detail: Council received the 2025 progress report on the city's strategic plan, which covers foundations, city building, environment, and people and the economy {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Staff said the data shows a challenging housing environment: rising costs and economic uncertainty slowed new construction to its lowest level in several years, though the city supported 26 affordable units.

On the conservation authority's Niska lands, one councillor asked whether surplus land might be used for affordable housing. The authority's representative said its board would consider the city's request at a special meeting on July 27.

Police said proactive work on human trafficking, including reviewing intimate partner violence cases, may raise reported crime figures. One councillor asked how to ensure the city gets credit for this work rather than blame.

Councillors asked the library about addiction-related incidents and the new daytime shelter. The library said the summer has been relatively incident-free, but it could not say for certain that the shelter was the cause.

Public health described using AI tools to automate records and letters so nurses spend more time with families. A councillor asked how the health unit achieves its high HPV vaccination rate, and staff said they rely on facts, school outreach and parent engagement.
